lessons.title: quid tibi nōmen est?, mihi nōmen est... — "what's your name?", the dative way
lessons.headword: quid tibi nōmen est? / mihi nōmen est...
lessons.romanization: quid tibi nōmen est? / mihi nōmen est...
lessons.gloss: what's your name? / my name is... — the genuinely classical dative of possession, literally what is the name to you?

segments.text: English says you have a name. German says you're called something. Latin does neither — it says the name belongs to you, using nothing but a case ending.

blocks.title: You'll want to know: quid tibi nōmen est? — literally "what is the name TO YOU?"

segments.text: Quid tibi nōmen est? ("what's your name?") is, word for word, "what [is] the-name [to] you?" — no verb for "have," no verb for "be called." The name simply exists, and tibi ("to you," dative case) says who it belongs to.

blocks.title: You'll want to know: mihi nōmen est... — the same construction, in reply

segments.text: The reply follows the identical pattern: mihi nōmen est [name] — "[the-name] [is] to-me [name]." This is Latin's genuine "dative of possession": instead of a possessive verb, the possessor simply sits in the dative case, and the thing possessed — here, nōmen, "name" — stays in the nominative, as the sentence's real subject.

segments.text: What case does the possessor sit in, in mihi nōmen est? (Dative — mihi, "to me.") Does Latin use a verb like "have" or "be called" for this? (No — the name simply exists; possession is shown by the dative case alone.) What noun remains the sentence's grammatical subject? (Nōmen, "name.")

lessons.title: Mārcus or Mārcō? — a real classical variation
lessons.gloss: the possessor stays dative, while classical authors vary between nominative and matching dative for the name itself

segments.text: The possessor in Latin's naming construction is reliably dative. The personal name beside nōmen, however, is not locked to one case in every author.
The dative possessor appears across authors from Plautus through Livy and Sallust:
puerō nōmen est... — to the boy the name is...
That puerō does not change. It marks the person who possesses the name.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: Two habits for the personal name

segments.text: Cicero tends to keep the personal name nominative, agreeing with nōmen, the sentence's subject:
Livy and Sallust more often pull the personal name into the dative to match the possessor:
The underlying dative-of-possession construction is the same. The choice between Mārcus and Mārcō is authorial variation, not evidence that one sentence has stopped using the dative of possession.

Which author tends toward nominative Mārcus? (Cicero.)
Which authors more often use matching dative Mārcō? (Livy and Sallust.)
Do the two forms represent different possession constructions? (No.)
